Paper Summary The paper applies Generalizability Theory to LLM evaluation variance across 5 benchmarks, 4–6 models, and multiple infrastructure × methodology factors (172,800–230,400 observations per experiment). It makes three claims: (1) item dominance estimates are sample-unstable (CV=33%), (2) model×item interaction (33%) is the largest overlooked component when model is treated as a crossed facet, and (3) D-study reproducibility budgets converge across benchmarks but carry ±190-item CIs rendering benchmark-specific recommendations meaningless. The framing: \"variance decomposition is a measurement, not a fact.\" 2. R1 Review: Methodology & Experiments Strengths -  Impressive experimental scale.  ~ 4M total records across 8 experiments, 5 benchmarks, 6 models. The factorial designs are well-constructed and the confound correction (V0 enforce_ eager) is a genuine contribution. -  Model-as-facet reanalysis is well-executed.  The item_ id drop from 37.8%→15.2% with model×item absorbing the difference is a clean, interpretable result that challenges standard practice. -  Separability analysis across hardware.  The infra×method jump from 1.5% (single-GPU) to 5.5% (multi-GPU) is well-demonstrated and practically important. -  D-study projections with uncertainty.  Reporting bootstrap CIs on reproducibility budgets is methodologically sound practice that prior work omits. Weaknesses -  Centerpiece claim rests on thin evidence.  The CV=33% finding (Exp 1b) uses only 3 item samples, 1 model (Llama-3.1-8B), 1 benchmark (MMLU). Three data points cannot reliably estimate a coefficient of variation. The CV itself has enormous uncertainty — it could plausibly be 15% or 50%. A claim that \"all prior single-decomposition studies over-commit\" requires far more resamples (30+ recommended) and generalization across models and benchmarks. -  Bootstrap validity concern.  Resampling 200 items with replacement creates ~ 127 unique items per bootstrap sample, producing duplicate observations that violate the independence assumptions of the G-theory model. The resulting CIs may be miscalibrated. The paper does not discuss this issue or compare with jackknife/subsampling alternatives. -  Cross-benchmark design asymmetry.  MMLU uses a 3×3 precision-temperature grid while other benchmarks use 2×2. Comparing variance percentages across different factorial structures without matched-design sensitivity analysis is methodologically questionable. -  G-coefficient interpretation.  The paper reports G=0.32 for 200 items as evidence of \"inherent low reliability,\" but standard MMLU evaluation uses all ~ 14K items. D-study projection to full benchmark size would likely yield G>0.90, substantially weakening the alarm about current practice. -  Zero figures.  A paper about variance decomposition with 18 tables and no figures is a critical presentation failure. Stacked bar charts, waterfall diagrams, and bootstrap density plots (all described in the design context) would dramatically improve comprehension. -  Thin secondary experiments.  Exp 5 (n=2 14B models, scale/architecture confounded) contributes near-zero evidential value. Exp 7 (LayerCast) is a null result that could be a footnote. Exp 6 (RoBERTa fine-tuning) uses encoder-only architecture, making the inference-training comparison apples-to-oranges for the LLM evaluation claim. Questions for Authors 1.  Why only 3 item resamples for the centerpiece claim? What is the bootstrap CI on the CV=0.33 estimate itself? 2.  How do you handle duplicate items in bootstrap resamples given G-theory's independence assumptions? 3.  What would G be for MMLU at its full ~ 14K item size under your D-study projections? 4.  The MMLU experiments use a richer factorial design than other benchmarks — have you verified that the cross-benchmark comparisons aren't confounded by design differences? R1 Score: 4/6 (Weak Accept) | Confidence: 4/5 3. R2 Review: Novelty & Related Work Strengths -  The resampling instability result is novel for ML evaluation.  Even if the concept is known in psychometrics, nobody has empirically demonstrated rank inversions across item samples for LLM evaluation variance decomposition. The qualitative finding (residual > item_ id in Sample 7) is striking. -  The bimodality→item_id correlation  (r=0.95) is an interesting mechanistic hypothesis that could guide benchmark design, even if underpowered (n=5 benchmarks). -  Engine confound correction  (V0 enforce_ eager reducing precision main effect from ~ 7% to 1.6%) is a valuable practical contribution for the community. -  Clear three-contribution structure  in the introduction makes claims easy to evaluate. Weaknesses -  The central conceptual claim is not novel.  \"Variance decomposition estimates have sampling variability\" is established in psychometric measurement theory (Brennan 2001, Chapter 8; Cardinet et al. 2010). The paper presents this as a discovery (\"we set out to build budgets and discovered the budget is unreliable\") without acknowledging that measurement theorists have known this for decades. For a measurement-literate audience, the surprise factor is low. -  Missing engagement with psychometric precedent.  The paper cites Shavelson & Webb (1991) and Brennan (2001) for G-theory basics but ignores their extensive discussion of variance component estimation error, sampling variability of G-coefficients, and the known sensitivity to universe definition (fixed vs. random facets). The critique of Mesting (2026) for treating model as fixed is particularly problematic — model-as-fixed is a legitimate design choice when generalizing only to those specific models, not an \"error.\" -  Three claims are one finding stated three ways.  All three contributions reduce to \"variance component estimates are uncertain\": (1) they vary across item samples, (2) they vary across model specifications, (3) the D-study projections derived from them are also uncertain. This is a single observation about estimation uncertainty, not three independent contributions. -  Purely diagnostic — no constructive contribution.  The three recommendations (report resampling stability, treat model as crossed, add CIs to budgets) are standard statistical advice. The paper does not provide a corrected estimation procedure, a practical resampling protocol, a software tool, or a concrete recommended minimum number of resamples. Practitioners reading this paper learn that their current approach is wrong but not what to do instead. -  The narrative pivot feels post-hoc. Methodology Assessment 2.1 G-Theory Application The application of G-theory is broadly correct and represents a natural fit for the research question. The crossed random-effects design, with item as the measurement facet and prompt/seed/temperature/ordering/precision as crossed facets, is the canonical G-theory setup for studying measurement dependability. The paper correctly distinguishes G-studies (variance decomposition) from D-studies (projection under alternative designs), which is the primary advantage of G-theory over standard ANOVA. However, there are several methodological concerns: (a) Object of measurement is underspecified.  In classical G-theory, the \"object of measurement\" (the entity whose score you want to generalize) must be clearly defined. In educational testing, this is typically the person. Here, the paper appears to treat benchmark accuracy as the object, but accuracy is an aggregate over items -- not a single observation. The paper decomposes item-level binary responses (correct/incorrect), which means the effective object of measurement is the  item-level response . The G coefficient then measures how well item-level responses generalize across facet conditions. This is a valid but nonstandard application. The paper should explicitly state what universe score is being estimated and what generalization is being made. The current framing conflates \"reliability of a benchmark score\" with \"stability of item-level responses across conditions,\" and these are different quantities. (b) Model-as-fixed vs. model-as-facet transition is handled well but incompletely.  The paper correctly identifies that pooling across models inflates item_ id (from 56% to 49.2% on MMLU when model is added as a facet). The model x item interaction (10.2%) is properly extracted. However, the paper does not discuss whether model should be treated as random or fixed from a G-theory perspective. With only 4 models drawn from a specific population (7-9B instruction-tuned open-weight models), the \"random\" assumption implies these 4 are a random sample from some universe of models -- a dubious claim given the deliberate selection. If model is fixed, model x item is not an error component but a systematic interaction, and the G coefficient computation changes. The paper should discuss this inferential scope issue. (c) Henderson Method I vs. III naming inconsistency.  The paper claims \"Henderson's Method III (expected mean squares)\" in Section 3.1, but the balanced fully-crossed design used here would typically employ Henderson Method I (which uses Type-I sums of squares and expected mean squares for balanced designs). Method III is Searle's approach for unbalanced designs. For the balanced design in exp-001, Method I is both simpler and more appropriate. This is either a naming error or an implementation concern -- the paper should clarify which method was actually used and verify consistency with the code. (d) Binary response variable creates floor/ceiling artifacts.  All primary analyses use binary correct/incorrect as the response. For items near 0% or 100% accuracy across conditions, variance is mechanically compressed (a Bernoulli variable with p near 0 or 1 has low variance). This means item_ id partially reflects the  range  of item difficulties rather than genuine measurement-relevant variance. The logprob analysis in Appendix B (item_ id drops to 42.8%) partially addresses this, but it is relegated to a 4-line appendix rather than being integrated into the main analysis. A continuous response variable would provide a more principled decomposition, and the paper should discuss the implications of using binary outcomes for variance component estimation. 2.2 Crossed/Nested Design Appropriateness The fully crossed design for MMLU (exp-001) is the gold standard for G-theory and is correctly specified. All facet levels are combined with all other facet levels, enabling clean estimation of all main effects and two-way interactions. The reduced designs for non-MMLU benchmarks (2 precisions x 2 temperatures vs. 3 x 3 for MMLU) are a pragmatic budget-driven decision but create a methodological asymmetry that is inadequately discussed. Variance percentages are  relative to total variance , and the total variance changes when you remove facet levels. Removing the FP32 precision level (which shows the highest deviation post-confound-fix) and the third temperature level changes the denominator of all percentage calculations. The cross-benchmark gradient (Table 4) compares percentages from designs with different factorial structures, which is a validity concern. With 200 items and replacement, each bootstrap draw contains approximately 127 unique items (by the coupon collector / birthday problem). Duplicate items have identical response vectors across all conditions, violating the independence assumption in the ANOVA decomposition. This likely  deflates  the variability of item_ id estimates (making CIs too narrow), because the resampled datasets have artificially correlated item effects. A cluster bootstrap that resamples item-condition blocks without re-indexing duplicates, or a delete-d jackknife, would be more appropriate. The tight CI widths (4-6pp) should be interpreted with this caveat. (b) Nested bootstrap for D-study projections is not described. CoT stochasticity shifts variance into temp×item and seed×item on reasoning tasks. 2.  Confirmatory separability null:  direct infra×methodology interactions  <0.3% under binary scoring on knowledge benchmarks, validating isolated-factor studies at the aggregate level. Over 3 million evaluation records are analyzed. Three claims are made: (1) a benchmark-conditional variance gradient where item dominance ranges from 48% (MMLU) to 28% (MATH) under model-as-facet analysis; (2) infrastructure x methodology separability at the aggregate level ( <0.5% on knowledge benchmarks, rising to 3% on math-generation benchmarks); (3) metric-conditional, benchmark-specific reproducibility budgets via D-study projections. Extensions cover 14B models, RoBERTa fine-tuning, LayerCast precision mitigation, and three scoring metrics. 2. Methodological Soundness 2.1 G-Theory Framework Application Largely correct, with one significant improvement over Dream #1.  The revised paper treats model as a crossed random facet (Section 4.4 / Table 5), which was the most critical methodological concern in the prior review. This properly separates model×item interaction (16-22%) from pure item variance and residual. The 4pp systematic reduction across all benchmarks is plausible and consistent with psychometric expectation when objects of measurement have heterogeneous difficulty profiles. Henderson Method III vs. REML.  The paper uses Henderson Method III (expected mean squares) as primary estimation with REML as sensitivity check. This is defensible: Henderson III is unbiased for balanced designs, and the design is nearly balanced (fully crossed within each experiment). The reported max divergence of 2.1pp with preserved rank ordering is reassuring. However: -  Concern:  Henderson Method III can produce negative variance component estimates for near-zero components. The MATH table (Table 22 in the imagined experiments) shows a negative \"other\" entry (-1.5%), which is characteristic of this issue. The paper should explicitly state how negative estimates are handled (set to zero? redistributed? left as-is?). This matters for the separability claim where infra×method components are near zero — a negative estimate truncated to zero looks different from a genuinely zero estimate. -  Concern:  The G-theory formula presented in Equation 2 is simplified. The actual D-study formula for a multi-facet crossed design with 5+ facets involves many more terms. The paper should either present the full formula used or cite a specific implementation (e.g., GeneralizIT package). The simplified formula risks misleading readers about how D-study projections were actually computed. 2.2 Crossed Random-Effects Assumptions Items as random facet:  Justified. The 200 items per benchmark are sampled (stratified) from larger pools (MMLU: 14,042; ARC: 2,590; GSM8K: 1,319; HellaSwag: 10,042; MATH: 5,000). The random-facet assumption requires that observed items are exchangeable draws from a universe of admissible observations. Stratified sampling strengthens this by ensuring subject/topic coverage. Model as random facet:  Partially justified. Four 7-9B models from different families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral) are treated as exchangeable draws from the universe of \"7-9B instruction-tuned LLMs.\" This is defensible but arguable — the model universe is not well-defined, and four models provide limited degrees of freedom for estimating model-related variance components. The 14B extension (2 models) is even more constrained. The paper should acknowledge that model-as-facet with k=4 yields imprecise estimates of model variance components and that the model universe is narrowly defined (open-weight, instruction-tuned, 7-9B). Prompt as random facet:  The 6 prompt templates are described but their generation process matters for the random-effects assumption. If they were systematically designed to vary specific dimensions (e.g., formality, instruction explicitness), they may not represent random draws from a prompt universe. The paper should clarify whether prompt templates were generated to be representative (supporting random effects) or to maximize diversity (which biases variance estimates upward). Seed as random facet:  Clearly justified — seeds are arbitrary integers drawn from a large space. Temperature as random facet:  Problematic. With only 2-3 levels (e.g., 0, 0.5, 1.0), treating temperature as a random facet is statistically dubious — these are specific points chosen to span the parameter range, not random draws from a temperature distribution. Temperature is better modeled as fixed. If treated as random, the variance estimates carry extreme uncertainty with 2-3 df. The paper should address this. Ordering as random facet:  Four orderings (ABCD, BCDA, CDAB, DABC) — these are systematic rotations, not random draws. The random-effects assumption is defensible only if one argues these represent exchangeable draws from the universe of possible orderings, which is reasonable for 4-option MC but should be noted. 2.3 Variance Estimation for Binary Data Critical methodological question.  Binary correct (0/1) data violates the normality assumption underlying standard G-theory variance component estimation. Henderson Method III and REML both assume continuous, approximately normal response variables. For binary data: -  Variance components are bounded by the Bernoulli variance p(1-p), creating ceiling effects for items near p=0 or p=1. -  Item-level variance is mechanically linked to item difficulty — easy and hard items contribute less variance by construction, inflating the apparent dominance of \"mid-difficulty\" items. -  The paper's finding that item_ id is the largest variance source is partially an artifact of using binary scoring on items with heterogeneous difficulty. This is the well-known \"item difficulty confound\" in classical test theory. The text-exact-match metric (also binary) and logprob metric (continuous) provide useful sensitivity checks. The logprob result (item_ id = 55%) is methodologically cleaner because the response variable is continuous, avoiding the binary data issue. The paper should discuss the binary data limitation explicitly and note that logprob scoring provides the most methodologically sound variance decomposition. 3. Experimental Design 3.1 Factorial Design Adequacy MMLU (Exp 1): Strong.  4 models × 3 precisions × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 items = 1,036,800 observations. This is the richest design and supports all claimed decompositions. The V0 enforce_ eager control eliminates the engine confound — this is excellent experimental hygiene. Cross-benchmark (Exp 3): Adequate but reduced.  2 precisions × 2 temperatures (vs. 3×3 on MMLU). The reduction is justified by compute constraints but creates an asymmetry: FP32 is absent from cross-benchmark experiments, meaning the precision facet is restricted to BF16/FP16 (which differ minimally). The claimed cross-benchmark gradient in precision effects (MMLU 3.0% vs. GSM8K 1.0%) is confounded with the different precision levels tested. This should be explicitly acknowledged. Multi-hardware (Exp 4): Adequate.  2 GPU types is the minimum for estimating hardware effects. With 1 df for hardware main effect, the estimate is necessarily imprecise. The paper correctly frames hardware findings as directional rather than definitive. Item resampling (Exp 2): Well-designed.  Three independent stratified draws with different seeds. The CV=0.19 (paper) or CV=0.19 (imagined experiments) on item_ id is an important honesty result. However, three draws provide only a rough estimate of resampling variability — 10+ draws would be more convincing, though the compute cost may be prohibitive. Fine-tuning (Exp 7): Adequate for its scope.  432 runs per task × 4 tasks = 1,728 total. The fully crossed design (seed × LR × shuffle × GPU × precision) is clean. The RoBERTa-large choice is acknowledged as a limitation (encoder-only, classification). This experiment is best framed as a conceptual extension rather than a direct generalization. 3.2 Missing Controls and Confounds 1.  Batch size / sequence length confound.  vLLM batches requests dynamically. If different benchmark items produce different output lengths (especially GSM8K/MATH with CoT), batch composition may vary, introducing an unmodeled variance source that gets absorbed into residual or item interactions. The paper uses \"default vLLM settings\" which is realistic but means batch-level nondeterminism is present. 2.  Prompt template × benchmark interaction.  The same 6 prompt templates are used across benchmarks, but their appropriateness may vary by task. A prompt template that works well for MMLU factual recall may be poorly suited for GSM8K math reasoning. This could inflate prompt×item interactions on some benchmarks for reasons unrelated to the \"prompt sensitivity\" construct. 3.  Item difficulty distribution differs across benchmarks.  MMLU items span a wide difficulty range; GSM8K items at 8B model scale cluster near 0.4-0.6 accuracy; MATH items are heavily bimodal (trivial or impossible for 8B models). These distributional differences mechanically affect how much variance is attributable to items vs. interactions. The paper's \"cognitive complexity\" explanation for the cross-benchmark gradient is plausible but not the only explanation — difficulty distribution differences could account for part of the pattern. 4.  Stratified sampling details.  The paper mentions stratified sampling across 57 MMLU subjects, but the stratification scheme for other benchmarks (GSM8K difficulty levels? MATH topics?) is not described. If non-MMLU benchmarks lack stratification, their item samples may be less representative. 5.  Answer extraction method.  For generation-based scoring, the method of extracting answers from generated text is a potential confound. Different regex/parsing strategies could produce different binary scores for the same generation. This is not discussed. 3.3 Item Sampling Strategy The 200-item stratified sample from MMLU's 14,042 items (1.4%) is a reasonable balance between compute cost and representativeness. The resampling stability test (CV=0.19) properly quantifies the sampling uncertainty. For other benchmarks: -  GSM8K: 200/1,319 = 15.2% — much denser sampling, less sampling uncertainty expected. -  ARC-Challenge: 200/2,590 = 7.7% — moderate. -  HellaSwag: 200/10,042 = 2.0% — similar to MMLU. -  MATH: 200/5,000 = 4.0% — moderate. The paper should note that cross-benchmark comparisons of item_ id variance share are confounded with sampling fraction — benchmarks with denser item sampling (GSM8K) mechanically have lower item-sampling uncertainty, which could affect the D-study projections. 4. Statistical Rigor 4.1 Bootstrap Confidence Intervals Construction:  1,000 item×condition resamples. This is a standard nonparametric bootstrap for G-theory (cf. Brennan, 2001, Ch. 10). The resampling unit matters: resampling items treats items as the primary sampling unit, which is appropriate given that item selection is the largest variance source. Concerns: -  The bootstrap resamples items but holds conditions (prompt, seed, temp, precision, ordering) fixed. This captures item-sampling uncertainty but not condition-sampling uncertainty. A more thorough approach would resample both items and conditions (double bootstrap), though this is computationally expensive and rarely done in G-theory applications. The paper should acknowledge this limitation. -  The reported CI widths (~ 0.14 for item_ id) are wide enough that the practical implications change substantially across the CI range. For example, MMLU item_ id [ 0.41, 0.55] maps to different D-study recommendations at each endpoint. The paper handles this well by reporting D-study CIs ([ 350, 510 ] for G≥0.90 on MMLU). 4.2 D-Study Projections Validity:  D-study projections assume that variance components estimated from the G-study generalize to the projected design. This is the standard G-theory assumption and is reasonable when the projected design changes only the number of levels (e.g., more items, more seeds) rather than the nature of the facets. The projections in Table 8 change item counts while holding prompt/seed counts at \"optimal\" levels — this is valid. Concern — optimal prompt/seed counts.  The D-study recommends \"3 prompts / 4 seeds\" for MMLU and \"4 prompts / 6 seeds\" for GSM8K. How are these \"optimal\" counts determined? If they are chosen to minimize total compute for a target G, the optimization procedure should be described. If they are chosen post-hoc to make the item counts look reasonable, this is problematic. Concern — extrapolation to 420+ items.  The G-study uses 200 items. Projecting to 420 items assumes linear scaling of the error reduction, which holds under the random-sampling model. However, if the additional 220 items are drawn from the same pool, they may not be independent of the original 200 (especially for smaller pools like GSM8K with only 1,319 total items). The finite-population correction should be applied when the projected sample is a large fraction of the universe. 4.3 REML Sensitivity Check Sufficient for its purpose.  The 2.1pp maximum divergence with preserved rankings is adequate evidence that the choice between Henderson III and REML does not affect qualitative conclusions. However, REML is generally preferred for unbalanced designs. Since the within-experiment designs are balanced (fully crossed), Henderson III is appropriate. The sensitivity check confirms this. 4.4 Permutation Test for Gradient The p=0.003 for the gradient direction (MMLU > HellaSwag on item_ id) is properly reported. The paper correctly notes that the CIs overlap partially at the margins ([ 0.38, 0.41 ]), supporting directional but not magnitude claims. This is honest and appropriate. 5. Reproducibility Concerns 1.  vLLM version dependency.  The paper uses vLLM 0.9.2 with V0 enforce_ eager. vLLM's behavior changes across versions (the V0/V1 engine confound demonstrates this). The results may not replicate on vLLM 0.8.x or 1.0.x. The paper should pin the exact vLLM commit hash, not just the version number. 2.  Model weight provenance.  The paper lists model names but not specific weight versions (e.g., HuggingFace revision hashes). Model weights on HuggingFace can be updated without changing the model card name. For reproducibility, exact weight hashes are needed. 3.  CUDA version and driver.  CUDA nondeterminism is a core topic of the paper. The exact CUDA version, cuDNN version, and driver version should be reported. The paper mentions \"CUDA 12.8\" support for vLLM 0.9.2 but does not pin the exact software stack. 4.  Item sample seeds.  The stratified sampling seeds for the 200-item samples should be released. The resampling stability test uses seeds 0, 7, 99 — are these the only seeds tested? If the main experiments use a single seed (e.g., seed 0), the results are conditional on that particular draw. 5.  Prompt template text.  The 6 prompt templates are critical to reproducibility but their exact text is not provided in the paper. They should appear in an appendix. 6. Strengths -  Comprehensive factorial design.  The MMLU experiment (1,036,800 observations, 5,184 conditions) is one of the largest crossed factorial designs in LLM evaluation research. The systematic approach — full crossing on MMLU, reduced crossing on other benchmarks, explicit confound controls — reflects careful experimental planning. -  Engine confound discovery and fix.  Identifying that default vLLM routes FP32 through a different engine (V1 CUDA graph) than BF16/FP16 (V0 eager) is a standalone methodological contribution. The enforce_ eager fix is simple, actionable, and immediately useful to the community. -  Model-as-facet analysis.  This revision correctly treats model as a crossed random facet, addressing the most fundamental concern from Dream #1. The systematic 4pp reduction across all benchmarks and the extraction of 16-22% model×item interaction is a clean result. -  Multi-benchmark coverage.  Five benchmarks spanning knowledge retrieval (MMLU, ARC), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag), arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K), and proof reasoning (MATH) provides genuine coverage of the LLM evaluation landscape. The three-tier clustering is more nuanced than a simple monotonic gradient. -  Metric-conditional analysis.  The binary/text-match/logprob comparison (Table 9) is a first-order finding: G ranges from 0.32 to 0.97 depending on the scoring metric. This alone justifies the paper — practitioners cannot discuss \"reliability\" without specifying the metric. -  Honest uncertainty quantification.  Bootstrap CIs on variance components, D-study CIs on item counts, resampling stability tests, and REML sensitivity checks collectively demonstrate statistical maturity. The paper acknowledges that the gradient is directional rather than precisely quantified. -  Three-tier narrative is stronger than two-cluster.  Including MATH extends the gradient from {MMLU, ARC} vs. {GSM8K, HellaSwag} to a three-tier structure with 20pp spread, providing more evidence for the benchmark-conditional story. -  Separability as confirmatory null.  Reframing infrastructure×methodology separability as a confirmatory result (validating prior isolated-factor studies) rather than a breakthrough is intellectually honest and strengthens the paper's credibility. -  Fine-tuning contrast.  The inverted variance hierarchy (LR/seed dominate in fine-tuning vs. items dominate in inference) adds conceptual depth and explains why different evaluation modes have different reproducibility conventions. 7. Weaknesses Major -  Binary data in G-theory.  Applying standard G-theory variance component estimation (Henderson III / REML) to binary (0/1) data is methodologically questionable. The response variable violates normality and homoscedasticity assumptions. Item variance is mechanically linked to item difficulty via the Bernoulli variance function. This affects the headline item_ id estimates and all downstream D-study projections. The logprob analysis partially mitigates this, but the paper's primary analysis is on binary data. A generalized G-theory approach (Brennan, 2001, Ch. 12) or a link-function-based decomposition would be more appropriate. At minimum, the paper must discuss this limitation and note that item dominance under binary scoring is partially artifactual. -  Temperature and ordering as random facets.  With 2-3 temperature levels and 4 systematic ordering rotations, treating these as random facets is questionable. Random-effects estimation requires the observed levels to be exchangeable draws from a larger universe. Temperature levels (0, 0.5, 1.0) are specific design points, not random draws from a temperature distribution. The 4 orderings are systematic rotations, not random permutations of 4 !=24 possibilities. Misspecifying fixed effects as random inflates the estimated variance components for these facets and their interactions. The paper should either (a) justify the random-effects assumption for these facets, (b) treat them as fixed and re-estimate, or (c) present both analyses as a sensitivity check. -  Asymmetric designs across benchmarks weaken cross-benchmark claims.  MMLU uses 3 precisions × 3 temperatures; other benchmarks use 2 × 2. FP32 is absent from non-MMLU experiments. This means precision-related variance on MMLU includes the FP32 degradation effect that is absent from other benchmarks. The claimed gradient in precision effects (MMLU 3.0% → MATH 0.5%) is confounded with the different precision levels tested. The paper should either (a) re-analyze MMLU restricted to BF16/FP16 for the cross-benchmark comparison, or (b) explicitly state the confound. -  Separability claim is benchmark-conditional but presented as a general finding.  The abstract and contributions list separability as \" <0.5% binary\" but the body reveals GSM8K reaches 3.0% and MATH reaches 2.5%. A finding that holds on 3/5 benchmarks but fails on 2/5 is not a general separability result — it is a benchmark-conditional one. The abstract and conclusions should lead with the conditionality. Moderate -  D-study \"optimal\" prompt/seed counts are not derived.  The paper presents specific prompt and seed counts (3/4 for MMLU, 4/6 for GSM8K) as \"optimal\" without showing the optimization procedure. Are these the minimum counts that don't substantially change the D-study item projection? Are they from a cost-minimization formula? The derivation matters because practitioners will use these numbers directly. -  Residual component is large and underanalyzed.  Residual ranges from 6% to 18% across benchmarks and analyses. Under model-as-facet analysis, the residual on MMLU drops from 14% to 8%, which is progress, but 8% is still substantial. What is in this residual? Higher-order interactions (3-way and above) are mentioned in passing (\"3-5% total\") but not tabulated. The paper claims higher-order interactions are small, but 3-5% is comparable to many named 2-way interactions (e.g., seed×item at 2.0%). An appendix breaking down the residual would strengthen the paper. -  HellaSwag clustering with GSM8K is not well-explained.  HellaSwag is a commonsense reasoning / sentence completion task, not a math reasoning task. Its item_ id (31%) places it in the same tier as GSM8K (36%), but its infra×method (0.3%) is similar to knowledge benchmarks. The paper groups them in a \"mid\" tier based on item_ id alone, but the infra×method pattern suggests HellaSwag behaves differently from GSM8K. The three-tier narrative is cleaner than the data fully support. -  14B extension is underpowered.  With only 2 models, model-as-facet analysis has essentially 1 df for model effects. The reported model×item = 25% (vs. 21% at 8B) could reflect the specific model pair chosen (dense vs. reasoning-distilled) rather than a scale effect. The paper should note that the 8B→14B comparison confounds scale with architecture diversity. -  No correction for multiple comparisons.  Many variance components are tested across many benchmarks and metrics. While the bootstrap CIs provide individual component uncertainty, no family-wise error correction is applied. The GSM8K infra×method CI [ 0.012, 0.048 ] excludes zero, but is this still significant after correcting for testing the same hypothesis on 5 benchmarks? Minor -  \"Over 3 million\" vs. \"over 4 million.\"  The abstract says \"over 3 million\"; the best-tier paper says \"over 4 million.\" The actual count should be computed and reported exactly. -  MATH \"other\" = -1.5%.  Negative variance component estimates should be flagged and the handling policy stated (see Section 2.1 above). -  LayerCast section (8.3) adds little.  The finding that LayerCast provides marginal benefit over BF16 is expected given that precision effects are already small. This could be condensed to 1-2 sentences or moved to an appendix. -  Table 5 (model-as-facet) shows \"---\" for MATH precision entries.  If precision was not tested on MATH (only BF16/FP16), this should be noted explicitly rather than with a dash. 8. Questions for Authors 1.  How are negative variance component estimates handled?  Henderson Method III can produce negative estimates for near-zero components. Are these set to zero, left negative, or redistributed? This affects the separability claim. 2.  What justifies treating temperature (2-3 levels) as a random rather than fixed facet?  With 3 specific design points, the random-effects assumption is questionable. Have you compared results with temperature as fixed? 3.  For the cross-benchmark comparison, have you re-analyzed MMLU restricted to BF16/FP16 only (excluding FP32)?  This would make the precision facet comparable across benchmarks and test whether the precision gradient survives. 4.  How were the \"optimal\" prompt and seed counts in the D-study determined?  Is there a formal optimization procedure, or were these chosen by inspection? 5.  The bootstrap resamples items but not conditions. Have you considered a double bootstrap (resampling both items and conditions)?  This would capture total uncertainty rather than just item-sampling uncertainty. 6.  How do you address the binary data issue in G-theory estimation?  Standard methods assume continuous responses. Have you considered generalized G-theory or a probit/logit link function approach? 7.  The paper claims \"current practice G<0.25 everywhere\" — what specific \"current practice\" configuration yields this?  Is this 1 prompt × 1 seed × 200 items × 1 temperature × 1 precision? The baseline should be precisely defined. 8.  For GSM8K and MATH, how were answers extracted from generated text?  The extraction method is a potential confound for binary scoring. 9.  Were the 6 prompt templates the same across all 5 benchmarks?  If so, were they designed for MC format specifically, and how appropriate are they for GSM8K/MATH generation tasks? 10.  The fine-tuning experiment uses item-level accuracy across test set items as the response variable, or run-level aggregate accuracy?  If aggregate, G-theory is applied to a single number per run (N=432), which is a very different statistical regime than item-level analysis (N=432×test_ items). 9. Minor Issues -  The G-theory formula in Eq. 2 uses subscript notation that conflates \"conditions\" into a single $c$ — for a 5-facet design, the full formula should be shown or a reference to the exact formula used should be provided. -  Table 6 (cross-benchmark) reports 384,000 obs for GSM8K/ARC/HellaSwag but the experimental design (4 models × 2 prec × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 2 temps × 4 orderings × 200 items) yields 4×2×6×6×2×4×200 = 230,400. The 384,000 figure is inconsistent — please verify. -  The paper switches between \"Henderson Method I\" (Section 4.6) and \"Henderson Method III\" (summary). These are different methods — please clarify which was used. -  Several tables show components that do not sum to 100% without explanation. A footnote about rounding and/or the treatment of negative estimates would help. -  The Related Work paragraph on training instability cites Dodge et al. (2020) but the bibliography entry has no venue information beyond \"arXiv preprint.\" -  The Lu et al. (2022) citation appears to be incorrect — the cited paper is about emergent abilities, not option ordering. Verify this reference. -  The Mesting (2026) bibliography entry says \"ACL\" but the literature map says \"arXiv.\" Verify the venue. 10. Score and Confidence Overall Score: 4/6 (Weak Accept) Confidence: High Justification The paper has substantially improved since Dream #1 by: (a) treating model as a crossed facet, (b) adding bootstrap CIs, (c) expanding to 5 benchmarks with a coherent three-tier narrative, (d) reframing infrastructure separability as confirmatory, (e) expanding the bibliography to 18 references (still below the 25+ target but much improved), and (f) acknowledging item dominance as psychometrically expected while emphasizing the benchmark-conditional gradient as the novel contribution. The cross-benchmark variance gradient — the central claim — is well-supported by data across five benchmarks, with honest uncertainty quantification (permutation p=0.003, directional not magnitude claims). The D-study reproducibility budgets fill a genuine practical gap. The metric-conditional finding (G=0.37 vs. G=0.97) is striking and immediately useful. Summary This paper applies Generalizability Theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation in a multi-benchmark setting, crossing infrastructure facets (numerical precision, GPU hardware) with methodology facets (prompt template, random seed, temperature, option ordering) and a measurement facet (item selection) across five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), six models (7--14B), and 4M+ evaluation records. Three claims are advanced: (1) a cross-benchmark variance gradient where item_ id share drops monotonically from 56% (MMLU) to 21% (MATH), with CoT stochasticity shifting variance into temperature x item and seed x item interactions; (2) a confirmatory separability null -- direct infrastructure x methodology interactions < 0.3%; (3) D-study protocol reversals showing MMLU is item-limited (420 items for G >= 0.90) while GSM8K is seed-limited (10 seeds), with current practice yielding G  < 0.25 everywhere. Extensions include 14B scale validation, a fine-tuning G-study with RoBERTa-large, and LayerCast precision mitigation. 2. Novelty Assessment Claim 1 (Cross-benchmark variance gradient): Moderate-to-high novelty. This is the paper's strongest novel contribution. No prior work has demonstrated a systematic, monotonic shift in variance structure across multiple benchmarks positioned along a reasoning-intensity continuum. The 35pp gradient from MMLU to MATH, with the mechanistic explanation via CoT stochasticity, is a genuine empirical finding that unifies apparently contradictory conclusions from prior single-benchmark studies (Sclar on prompt sensitivity, Pezeshkpour on ordering, Yuan on precision). The \"unifying explanation\" framing is well-executed: these studies are not contradictory -- they studied different benchmarks at different positions on the gradient. However, the finding that item_ id dominates is expected from measurement theory (Brennan, 2001, Ch. 3). Any assessment instrument with wide difficulty range will show item variance as the largest source. The paper now acknowledges this appropriately (unlike the earlier draft), but the contribution is in the quantification and the gradient, not in item dominance per se. Claim 2 (Confirmatory separability): Low novelty, moderate utility. This is a confirmatory null result. Infrastructure x methodology interactions are  < 0.3% -- meaning that the infrastructure crossing, which the paper positions as a key methodological advance over Mesting (2026), yields almost nothing. The paper is now honest about this (framing it as \"confirmatory\" rather than \"discovery\"), which is the right move. The nuanced decomposition into direct vs. item-conditional interactions (Table 6) adds value: aggregate separability holds, but both factor types interact with items. This is useful methodological validation, but it does not constitute a primary novelty claim. The practical implication is clear: researchers running isolated-factor studies (e.g., studying only prompt sensitivity) can trust their aggregate conclusions, but should be cautious about item-level generalizations. This is valuable guidance even if not surprising. Claim 3 (D-study protocol reversal): Moderate novelty, high practical value. The finding that MMLU needs 420 items while GSM8K needs 10 seeds -- and that the facet effectiveness ratio inverts from 14.2:1 (MMLU) to 0.8:1 (GSM8K) -- is actionable and non-obvious. The \"no universal recipe\" conclusion directly challenges the standardized evaluation protocols being adopted by leaderboards. The D-study projection grids (Tables 9-10) are the most practically useful output of the paper. The current-practice G  < 0.25 finding is alarming and newsworthy, though its impact depends on whether the community adopts G-theory as a reliability metric. The comparison to educational measurement's G >= 0.80 threshold is effective rhetoric. Collective novelty: The three claims together are stronger than any individual claim. The cross-benchmark gradient (Claim 1) explains the protocol reversal (Claim 3), and the separability null (Claim 2) validates the independent study of each factor type. The narrative coherence is good. The paper is best understood as a large-scale empirical study that applies a well-established framework (G-theory) to a new domain (multi-benchmark LLM evaluation) and discovers a systematic empirical regularity (the gradient). This is a meaningful contribution, though not a methodological breakthrough. Incrementality over Mesting (2026). The paper clearly advances over Mesting in three dimensions: (a) five benchmarks vs. one, (b) infrastructure crossing, (c) model as crossed facet. The infrastructure crossing yields near-null results, so (b) is a confirmatory contribution. The multi-benchmark gradient and model-as-facet analysis are the genuine advances. The paper's four stated differences from Mesting (Section 2, paragraph 3) are accurate and honest. One important difference the paper does not sufficiently emphasize: Mesting found judge identity as the dominant variance source (43.8%), while this paper fixes the judge and finds item_ id dominant. These are complementary findings -- Mesting's design includes judge variance that would dominate everything else; this paper's design excludes judge to reveal the item/methodology/infrastructure structure underneath. This complementarity should be discussed more explicitly. 3. Related Work Completeness The bibliography has improved dramatically from the earlier 7-reference draft to 22 references. The four Related Work paragraphs are well-organized and the positioning against prior work is largely fair and accurate. Adequately covered: -  Variance sources in LLM evaluation (Sclar, Pezeshkpour, Lu, Yuan, Biderman) -- good coverage -  ANOVA-based decomposition (Bouthillier, Henderson, Dodge, Sellam, Dehghani) -- well-positioned -  G-theory in NLP (Mesting, Brennan, Shavelson) -- properly cited with explicit differentiation -  IRT in NLP (Lalor, Rodriguez, Polo, Perlitz) -- good, with IRT/G-theory complementarity noted Missing or under-discussed references: 1.  Nalisnick et al. (2024), GeneralizIT  -- a G-theory software package for ML. Directly relevant to the question of whether this paper's analytical framework is novel or already available as a tool. Should be cited in the G-theory paragraph. 2.  Kunievsky et al. (2025), prompt sensitivity decomposition  -- decomposes prompt variance into intent/articulation/model uncertainty. Relevant to interpreting the prompt x item interaction component. The paper's related_ work_ notes mention it but the paper does not cite it. 3.  Brittlebench (2026)  -- prompt brittleness benchmark, ~ 50% prompt variance. In the project's own literature map but absent from the paper. Directly relevant to the prompt facet findings. 4.  Bui et al. (2025), seed sensitivity in fine-tuning  -- RoBERTa/Llama seed sensitivity study. Directly relevant to Section 8.2 (fine-tuning G-study). In the literature map but not cited. 5.  ThinkingMachines (2025), batch invariance failure  -- 80/1000 unique completions at T=0 from batch-size dependence. The paper uses default vLLM settings without batch-invariant kernels; this reference would explain why seed x item effects are non-zero even at T=0. Not cited. 6.  Vania et al. (2021)  -- IRT item properties in NLP. Listed in the bibliography but not discussed in the Related Work text. Should be integrated into the IRT paragraph. 7.  Mizrahi et al. (2024)  -- cited in the introduction but not in Related Work. Multi-prompt evaluation advocacy. Should appear in the variance sources paragraph. Positioning fairness: The paper's positioning against prior work is generally fair. The claim that \"each prior study isolates at most two variance sources\" is accurate for the cited studies. The differentiation from Mesting is honest and specific. The IRT/G-theory complementarity framing is appropriate and avoids dismissing IRT work. One concern: the paper states that prior ANOVA-based studies \"lack the D-study machinery for projecting reliability under alternative designs.\" This is technically true but slightly misleading -- bootstrap-based approaches can achieve similar projections without G-theory. The advantage of D-study is its closed-form projections, not that the question is unanswerable otherwise. 4. Significance and Impact Will this paper change how people evaluate LLMs? Partially. The D-study budgets are immediately actionable for benchmark designers and evaluation framework maintainers (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness, HELM). The \"G  < 0.25 everywhere\" finding is a compelling indictment of current practice. However, adoption depends on: 1.  Whether the community accepts G-theory as the right reliability framework (vs. IRT, bootstrap, or simple confidence intervals) 2.  Whether the computational cost of multi-seed, multi-prompt evaluation is acceptable 3.  Whether leaderboard operators are incentivized to change practices The paper would benefit from a concrete comparison: \"Running MMLU with the recommended budget (420 items, 3 prompts, 2 seeds = 2,520 evaluations) costs X GPU-hours per model, compared to Y GPU-hours for current practice.\" Without cost estimates, the budgets are theoretical. Are the D-study budgets practically useful? Yes, with caveats. The specific numbers (420 items for MMLU, 10 seeds for GSM8K) are directly useful. The facet effectiveness ratios (Table 12) provide a decision framework. The projection grids (Tables 9-10) allow practitioners to find their own cost-reliability tradeoff. The main limitation is that the budgets are derived from 7-14B open-weight models. API-based models (GPT-4, Claude) may have different variance structures due to opaque infrastructure, quantization, and routing. The paper acknowledges this but does not quantify the risk. Is \"no universal recipe\" surprising or obvious? Moderately surprising in its specificity. The qualitative intuition that \"different benchmarks might need different protocols\" is not new. But the quantitative demonstration that the facet effectiveness ratio inverts from 14.2:1 to 0.8:1 across benchmarks, and that the same practitioner should use 420 items + 2 seeds for MMLU but 150 items + 10 seeds for GSM8K, is non-obvious and actionable. The counter-intuitive finding that knowledge benchmarks yield lower G than reasoning benchmarks (MMLU 0.36 vs. GSM8K 0.55 under full factorial) is genuinely surprising and well-explained. 5. Framing and Narrative Strengths: -  The three-claim structure is clean and well-supported. -  The \"unifying explanation\" framing for the gradient is effective. -  The Discussion section is balanced, with a thorough Limitations paragraph. -  The engine confound discovery is presented with appropriate before/after validation. -  The paper correctly frames infrastructure crossing as confirmatory rather than primary novelty. Weaknesses: -  Zero figures.  This is a serious deficiency for a variance decomposition paper. The distilled writing patterns from this field identify stacked-bar charts as an expected idiom (Mesting, Brittlebench). The cross-benchmark gradient (Table 5) would be far more compelling as a stacked-bar figure. The D-study projections (Tables 9-10) cry out for line plots of G vs. facet allocation. The facet effectiveness inversion (Table 12) would be intuitive as a crossing-lines plot. With 14 tables and 0 figures, the paper is dense and visually monotonous. This is a competitive disadvantage at a top venue. -  The paper title promises \"Evaluation Metrics\" but delivers only binary scoring.  The abstract and main text focus entirely on binary correct scoring. Logprob-based scoring is relegated to a one-paragraph appendix (Appendix B). The paper framing documents mention \"metric-conditional budgets\" as a core claim, but the submitted paper has largely abandoned this dimension. Either deliver the metric analysis or remove \"Evaluation Metrics\" from the title. -  The fine-tuning section (8.2) feels bolted on.  RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on SST-2/MNLI/RTE/COPA is architecturally distant from the 7-14B decoder inference setting. The variance hierarchy comparison (Table 15) is interesting but the cross-paradigm generalization is weak. This section would be stronger as a standalone follow-up study or should be explicitly qualified as \"preliminary evidence.\" 6. Scope Concerns Is 5 benchmarks x 6 models x 7-14B sufficient? For the cross-benchmark gradient: yes, 5 benchmarks spanning knowledge-to-reasoning is adequate. The monotonic gradient with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs (Table 8) provides statistical support. Adding more benchmarks (e.g., GPQA, TruthfulQA, HumanEval) would strengthen the gradient but is not strictly necessary. For model generality: the 4 x 7-9B models show consistent patterns (per-model tables confirm the gradient within each model), and the 14B extension (Section 8.1) falls within the 8B range. However: 1.  No 70B+ models.  Larger models may have qualitatively different variance structures (e.g., higher accuracy compresses item_ id, stronger reasoning reduces CoT stochasticity). The paper cannot claim generality beyond the 7-14B scale. 2.  No proprietary API models.  GPT-4, Claude, Gemini have opaque infrastructure (unknown precision, routing, batching). The separability null may not hold when infrastructure is uncontrolled. Mesting (2026) studied API models; this paper studies open-weight models. The complementarity is noted but not deeply explored. 3.  No non-English benchmarks.  All five benchmarks are English-only. Cross-lingual variance structure could differ systematically (e.g., tokenization effects on item difficulty). 4.  No generation-based benchmarks.  All benchmarks are multiple-choice or short-answer. Open-ended generation tasks (summarization, translation, creative writing) may have fundamentally different variance structures where temperature and seed effects dominate even more. 5.  Only 200 items per benchmark.  MMLU has ~ 14K items, GSM8K has ~ 8K. The 200-item stratified sample captures the difficulty distribution but may miss tail effects. The resampling stability test (Section 4.3) partially addresses this but only for MMLU. 7. Strengths (bulleted) -  Cross-benchmark variance gradient is a genuine, well-supported empirical contribution  that unifies contradictory findings from prior single-benchmark studies. The monotonic 35pp gradient from MMLU to MATH, with mechanistic explanation via CoT stochasticity, is the paper's signature finding. -  Massive experimental scale : 4M+ evaluation records, 5 benchmarks, 6 models, crossed factorial designs. Few empirical papers in this area match the breadth. -  D-study reproducibility budgets are immediately actionable : specific item/prompt/seed allocations for G >= 0.90, benchmark-specific, with projection grids for cost-reliability tradeoffs. -  Engine confound discovery and correction  (vLLM V0 vs. V1 routing for different precisions) is a standalone methodological contribution valuable to any researcher comparing precision modes. -  Honest framing of the separability null : infrastructure crossing framed as confirmatory rather than primary novelty, with nuanced decomposition into aggregate vs. item-conditional interactions. -  Comprehensive robustness checks : item resampling stability, REML vs. Henderson III comparison, bootstrap CIs, per-model breakdowns, 14B scale validation, cross-estimation-method concordance. -  Bibliography substantially improved  over earlier drafts: 22 references covering variance sources, ANOVA decomposition, G-theory, and IRT literature. -  Counter-intuitive G pattern  (knowledge benchmarks yield lower G than reasoning benchmarks) is well-explained and adds insight beyond the headline gradient finding. 8. Weaknesses (bulleted) -  Zero figures in a variance decomposition paper  is a serious presentation deficiency. Stacked-bar charts, D-study curves, and gradient visualizations are expected field idioms (Mesting 2026, Brittlebench 2026). 14 tables + 0 figures makes the paper dense and hard to scan. -  Infrastructure crossing is the claimed methodological advance over Mesting but yields near-null results  ( < 0.3% direct interactions). The main findings (gradient, D-study budgets) would emerge from a Mesting-style design with fixed infrastructure. The paper is honest about this but it weakens the novelty argument. -  Title promises \"Evaluation Metrics\" but the paper delivers only binary scoring  in the main text. Logprob analysis is a one-paragraph appendix. The metric-conditional dimension from the paper framing is largely absent. -  No models above 14B.  Larger models may compress item_ id and reduce CoT stochasticity, potentially altering the gradient. Generality claims should be scoped to 7-14B. -  Fine-tuning extension (RoBERTa-large, encoder-only, classification)  is architecturally distant from the decoder inference setting. Cross-paradigm generalization is weak; the section feels appended rather than integrated. -  Missing references : GeneralizIT (2024), Kunievsky et al. (2025), Brittlebench (2026), Bui et al. (2025), ThinkingMachines (2025) -- all in the project's own literature map but absent from the paper. These are relevant to the G-theory tooling, prompt decomposition, and fine-tuning variance discussions. -  No cost analysis for recommended budgets.  The D-study projections recommend specific item/prompt/seed allocations but do not estimate the GPU-hour cost of implementing these recommendations. Without cost, the budgets are theoretical. -  200-item samples from much larger benchmarks.  Resampling stability is tested only for MMLU. The other four benchmarks lack resampling validation, leaving open the possibility that the gradient is partially driven by item sampling artifacts on specific benchmarks. 9. Questions for Authors 1.  The cross-benchmark gradient is your strongest finding. Could you demonstrate that it holds under logprob-based scoring as well? The one-paragraph Appendix B suggests item_ id drops to 42.8% on MMLU, but does the full gradient (MMLU > ARC > HellaSwag > GSM8K > MATH) hold under logprob scoring? How does this compare to Polo et al.'s tinyBenchmarks recommendation for MMLU? If IRT-based subsampling achieves reliable rankings with fewer items, what does G-theory add? 3.  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B shows elevated temperature x item (8.8%) and seed x item (5.2%) on MMLU -- above the 8B range (Table 13). You attribute this to \"reasoning distillation introducing implicit chain-of-thought tendencies.\" Can you verify this mechanistically? Does DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B produce longer or more variable outputs on MMLU items compared to the other models? 4.  The separability null holds for 2 GPU types (Section 6). How confident are you that this extends to, say, A100 vs. H100 vs. B200 comparisons where the architectural differences (TF32 tensor cores, FP8 support, different memory bandwidth) are more substantial than between two GPUs of similar generation? 5.  You fix the judge model, unlike Mesting who includes judge as a facet. Since Mesting found judge identity as the dominant source (43.8%), your entire variance structure sits \"underneath\" the judge variance. How should practitioners interpret your budgets if they use LLM-as-judge evaluation (increasingly common)? Would your gradient hold if judge were included as a facet, or would judge variance dominate and flatten the cross-benchmark differences? 6. The paper uses Henderson's Method III with REML as sensitivity check and reports they agree within 1.4pp. Have you considered Bayesian variance component estimation (e.g., via Stan or brms)? This would give full posterior distributions on variance components rather than point estimates + bootstrap CIs, and would handle the near-zero infrastructure components more gracefully. 10. Clarify. -  Table 1 (MMLU variance): the \"infra x method\" row aggregates multiple interaction terms. Break this out or provide the individual terms in an appendix. -  The paper references \"Section 7\" (comprehensive analysis) as Section \\ref{sec:comprehensive} but the numbering in the LaTeX may not match if figures are added later. Verify cross-references. -  Appendix C on higher-order interactions is interesting (temp x seed x item = 1.8%) but could be expanded. Does this three-way interaction show a benchmark gradient similar to the two-way interactions? 11. Large-scale factorial design : 4 models × 5 benchmarks with multiple crossed facets represents the most comprehensive G-theory study in LLM evaluation to date. Float32 confound discovery : The identification of vLLM V1/V0 backend routing as a confound that inflated item variance from 24% to 58% is a standalone methodological contribution. The finding that learning rate dominates (17.8%) with a 10% lr×seed interaction, and inference-training decorrelation (r=0.15), are new and useful. 5.  D-study projections are practically useful : Showing that optimal allocations diverge qualitatively across benchmarks (MMLU: more items; GSM8K: more seeds) is actionable advice. Weaknesses : 1.  Residual dominance is the paper's Achilles heel  (Tables 1, 3, 5). Residual is the largest component on ALL benchmarks (20–40%). Combined with the opaque \"all other\" category (26.5% in Table 1), over 54% of MMLU variance is unexplained or aggregated. For a paper whose contribution is variance  attribution , having the majority of variance  unattributed  is a serious problem. The paper does not adequately discuss what these missing sources might be, nor does it attempt higher-order interaction estimation to decompose the residual. 2.  No confidence intervals or uncertainty quantification . Variance component estimates are reported as point estimates without bootstrap CIs, jackknife intervals, or any measure of estimation uncertainty. G-theory provides standard methods for this (Brennan 2001, Ch. 8). Without CIs, we cannot assess whether the differences between benchmarks or models are statistically meaningful or within estimation noise. For example, is item_ id=24% on MMLU vs 22% on ARC a real difference or sampling variability? 3.  Single GPU architecture severely limits \"infrastructure\" claims . Experiment 3 (multi-hardware) was blocked. The paper's title and framing reference \"infrastructure\" factors, but only numerical precision on one GPU type was tested. The finding that \"direct infrastructure×methodology interaction  < 0.5%\" (Table 4) applies only to precision, not hardware broadly. This should be reflected in the title/abstract. 4.  Model is not treated as a G-theory facet . The per-model decompositions (Table 1) show item_ id ranging from 13.8% (Mistral) to 30.2% (Gemma), suggesting strong model×item interaction. But model is analyzed as a stratification variable, not a facet in the G-study design. A model-as-facet reanalysis of the existing MMLU data (no new experiments needed) would properly attribute this variance and likely reduce the residual. 5.  Fine-tuning G-study uses RoBERTa-large  — an encoder-only model from 2019 — on classification tasks. The relevance to modern LLM fine-tuning (decoder-only models, generation tasks, RLHF/DPO) is questionable. The paper acknowledges this in Limitations but the mismatch weakens the \"fine-tuning contribution\" claim substantially. 6.  200 items per benchmark : While adequate for point estimation, the paper does not report sensitivity analyses (e.g., split-half reliability of the variance decomposition, or bootstrap resampling of items) to establish stability. Different 200-item samples from the same benchmark could yield different decompositions, especially for benchmarks with heterogeneous item pools. 7.  REML vs actual estimation method : The paper states \"Variance components are estimated via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML)\" (Section 3.1) but does not describe the actual implementation. If Henderson Method I (ANOVA-based) was used instead, this is a methodological misrepresentation that matters when variance components are near zero (negative estimates under Henderson are truncated differently than under REML). Questions for Authors : 1.  Can you provide bootstrap CIs (e.g., 1000 resamples of items) for the variance components in Tables 1 and 3? How much of \"all other\" and \"residual\" is actually model×item interaction? 3.  What specific variance estimation method was implemented? REML, Henderson I, or Henderson III? 4.  Have you examined three-way interactions (e.g., model×prompt×item) that might explain the large residual? The main findings are that item selection dominates variance (42-58%), infrastructure and methodology are separable at the aggregate level but interact through item difficulty, and D-study projections show current practices are severely underpowered (G  < 0.40). The work directly extends Mesting et al. (2026), who applied G-theory to methodological facets only, by adding infrastructure facets and testing separability. While the experimental scale is impressive (2M+ records, 5 benchmarks, 6 models), the novelty is incremental over Mesting, the item dominance finding is largely predictable from psychometric first principles, and the related work has significant gaps. Strengths S1.  Well-motivated separability test with nuanced outcome.  The distinction between aggregate separability ( <0.5% direct interactions) and item-conditional non-separability (14.2% combined) is genuinely useful. This is the paper's strongest conceptual contribution — it provides a principled answer to whether isolated-factor studies are valid, with appropriate caveats. The two-level framing (aggregate license + item-conditional warning) is more informative than a binary separability verdict. S2.  Scale and breadth of the experimental design.  Crossing 7 facets across 6 models, 5 benchmarks, and 2M+ records is a substantial empirical effort. The cross-benchmark gradient (item dominance decreasing with task difficulty, from 58.4% on MMLU to 42.1% on MATH) is a non-obvious finding that adds genuine insight about why reasoning benchmarks produce less reproducible results. S3.  Engine confound discovery.  The identification that vLLM routes FP32 through a different compute path than BF16/FP16, inflating precision variance from 0.3% to 0.87% (and precision x item from 1.8% to 7.24%), is a concrete methodological contribution of independent value. This is actionable for anyone doing precision comparisons and illustrates how infrastructure confounds can systematically bias variance attribution. S4.  D-study budgets are actionable.  The 10:1 marginal effectiveness ratio (items vs. prompts) and specific budget recommendations (600 items + 3 prompts + 2 seeds for G >= 0.90) translate directly into evaluation design guidance. The cross-benchmark budget table (550-1100 items depending on task) adds practical value. S5.  Fine-tuning extension broadens scope.  Showing that item dominance persists in fine-tuning (37-45%) while the secondary variance hierarchy shifts (seed/LR replace prompt/temperature) demonstrates the framework's generality beyond inference evaluation. Weaknesses W1.  Incremental novelty over Mesting et al. (2026).  The paper's core methodological contribution — applying G-theory to LLM evaluation — is Mesting's. What this paper adds is (a) infrastructure facets and (b) the separability test. But infrastructure turns out to be nearly negligible: precision contributes 0.3% main effect and hardware 0.6%. The separability test yields a largely expected null result at the aggregate level (it would be surprising if GPU type x prompt template interacted strongly). The item-conditional nuance is more interesting but is a secondary finding. The paper risks appearing as \"Mesting + two more facets that turn out not to matter much.\" W2.  Item dominance is predictable from psychometric first principles.  In any assessment with heterogeneous item difficulty, item variance will dominate when other factors have small effects. MMLU items range from trivial recall to expert reasoning — of course this produces massive item variance. The paper's own Discussion section essentially explains why this must be the case (\"steep difficulty gradient within every benchmark\"). The 58% figure quantifies what psychometricians would predict qualitatively. The paper does not adequately engage with whether this finding is genuinely surprising vs. a confirmation of well-known measurement theory. The counter-argument in the paper framing doc (\"the magnitude was not previously quantified\") is weak — the magnitude is a function of the specific item difficulty distribution in these benchmarks, not a universal property of LLM evaluation. W3.  Significant related work gaps.  Several important bodies of work are missing: -  Classical G-theory beyond Cronbach 1972.  Brennan (2001, \"Generalizability Theory\") is the standard modern reference and is entirely absent. Shavelson & Webb (1991) is missing. The median paper draft cites Brennan but the best-case paper does not. This is a serious omission for a paper whose primary methodological framework is G-theory. -  Reproducibility in ML broadly.  Pineau et al. (2021, \"Improving Reproducibility in ML: A Report from the NeurIPS Reproducibility Program\") and the ML reproducibility checklist literature are not cited. Bouthillier et al. (2021, \"Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks\") directly decomposed hyperparameter vs. seed vs. dataset variance using ANOVA — this is the closest ML-native predecessor to the present work and is completely missing. -  IRT-based item analysis in NLP.  Item Response Theory is the dominant psychometric framework for item analysis, and there is growing work applying IRT to NLP benchmarks (e.g., Lalor et al. 2019; Rodriguez et al. 2021 on IRT for NLP evaluation; Vania et al. 2021). The paper's finding that item selection dominates would be enriched by connecting to IRT-based difficulty estimation. -  Prompt ordering sensitivity.  Lu et al. (2022, \"Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them\") is a seminal work on ordering effects in LLM evaluation. The paper includes ordering as a facet but does not cite this foundational work. -  Benchmark contamination and item difficulty.  The item dominance finding intersects with work on benchmark contamination (Jacovi et al. 2023; Deng et al. 2024) and adaptive/dynamic benchmarking, which are not discussed. -  Variance decomposition in deep learning.  Beyond Bouthillier, there is work by Henderson et al. (2018, \"Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters\") on seed sensitivity and Dodge et al. (2020) on fine-tuning instability, both performing variance decomposition without G-theory. W4.  Positioning vs. Mesting is incomplete.  The paper claims to \"extend\" Mesting by adding infrastructure facets, but does not adequately address key differences: (a) Mesting included judge as a facet (43.8% variance), which this paper deliberately excludes — this makes the variance structures incomparable, and the paper's item dominance finding might not hold if judge were included; (b) Mesting studied API models with opaque infrastructure, while this paper studies open-weight models — the papers study fundamentally different evaluation settings; (c) the paper does not discuss whether its variance estimates are consistent with Mesting's for the overlapping facets (prompt, seed, temperature, item). A direct numerical comparison on shared facets would strengthen the positioning. W5.  D-study budgets are a straightforward computation, not a conceptual contribution.  Once variance components are estimated, D-study projections are a mechanical application of G-theory formulas (plug in different facet levels, compute G). Calling this a \"practical tool\" contribution overstates it — it is the standard output of any G-study. The novelty is in the variance component estimates, not in the D-study arithmetic. W6. The incremental \"first\" is adding hardware and precision facets to an existing G-theory framework. Similarly, \"first formal test of separability\" is a stretch — any multi-factor ANOVA implicitly tests interactions, which is the same as separability. The paper does not discuss this design choice or its implications. Questions for Authors Q1. How would the variance decomposition change if model were treated as a random facet rather than fixed? Specifically, what fraction of the current \"item_ id\" variance would be absorbed by model x item interactions? This is critical because the item dominance claim (58.4%) may be inflated by pooling across models with different difficulty profiles. Q2. Can you provide a direct numerical comparison with Mesting et al. (2026) on overlapping facets? The multi-hardware G-study reports exactly 0.5% for direct interactions — right at the threshold — which warrants sensitivity analysis. Q5. The paper treats \"item selection\" as a single construct, but items vary in multiple dimensions (difficulty, domain, format, discrimination). Can you decompose item variance further — e.g., into difficulty, domain, and residual item components? This would make the \"prioritize item count\" recommendation more actionable (should practitioners sample more items within domains, or across domains?). Q6. Bouthillier et al. (2021) conducted ANOVA-based variance decomposition across datasets, hyperparameters, and seeds for ML benchmarks generally. How do your findings compare? Their work predates yours and covers similar ground using simpler methods. What does G-theory add beyond what ANOVA decomposition already provides? Minor Issues M1. The bibliography has only 7 entries for a paper of this scope. A related work section citing only 7 papers at a top venue will raise immediate red flags. Expect 30-50 references minimum. M2. The title is 22 words long and contains a colon, a subtitle, and a methodological term. Consider shortening — e.g., \"Reproducibility Budgets for LLM Evaluation via Generalizability Theory.\" M3. The abstract mentions \"over 2 million evaluation records\" but the experiments sum to approximately 2.7M records. Be precise. M4. The term \"empirical license\" for isolated-factor studies is loaded — it suggests this paper has authority to grant permission to other researchers. Consider \"empirical support for\" instead. M5. Table 1 reports residual at 16.8% — this is a large unexplained component. The paper should discuss what residual captures (higher-order interactions, measurement error, model-level stochasticity beyond seed). M6. The paper should clarify the terminological mapping from psychometrics to ML evaluation more carefully. M7. The fine-tuning G-study uses RoBERTa-large, a 355M encoder model, which is architecturally very different from the 7-14B decoder models in the inference experiments. The generalizability of fine-tuning findings to modern LLM fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA on 7B+ models) is questionable. M8. Cronbach et al. (1972) citation is to the book \"The Dependability of Behavioral Measurements\" but the correct G-theory foundational reference is Cronbach, Gleser, Nanda & Rajaratnam (1972), which the paper does cite correctly in the bib — but should verify the title matches.
