The core finding is that item selection dominates variance (42-58%), direct infrastructure x methodology interactions are negligible (<0.5%), and current evaluation practices yield unacceptably low generalizability (G <0.40). D-study projections provide actionable reproducibility budgets. The methodology is largely sound and the experimental coverage is impressive, but several issues with estimation, design balance, generalizability claims, and missing analyses prevent a higher score. Strengths S1.  Correct and well-motivated G-theory application.  The paper properly applies REML estimation for variance component extraction in a random-effects framework. The choice of G-theory over simpler ANOVA decomposition is well-justified: it enables simultaneous multi-facet decomposition and D-study projections, which are the paper's key practical contribution. The universe score / relative error decomposition for the G coefficient follows standard Brennan (2001) formulations. S2.  Engine confound identification is a genuine methodological contribution.  The discovery that vLLM routes FP32 through a different compute path than BF16/FP16 (inflating precision variance from 0.3% to 0.87% main, 1.8% to 7.24% interaction) is valuable to the community independent of the G-theory framing. The fix (V0 enforce_ eager for all precision modes) is principled and well-documented. This demonstrates the kind of careful confound control that is often missing in LLM evaluation studies. S3.  Comprehensive experimental coverage.  All 8 planned experiments are reflected in the paper, covering: multi-model (6 models), multi-benchmark (5 benchmarks), multi-hardware (2 GPU types), scale validation (14B), paradigm extension (fine-tuning), and precision mode analysis (LayerCast). The total record count (>2M) provides substantial statistical power. The cross-benchmark gradient (item_ id share decreasing with task difficulty) is a genuinely interesting finding. S4.  Actionable D-study budgets.  The reproducibility budget tables (Tables 7-8) translate abstract variance components into concrete practitioner guidance. The \"10x more effective to triple items than triple prompts\" headline is well-supported by the marginal effectiveness ratios and will be immediately useful to evaluation practitioners. S5.  Appropriate use of generation-based evaluation.  Following Hua et al. (2025) to avoid log-likelihood scoring artifacts is a sound design choice that strengthens the ecological validity of the findings. Weaknesses W1.  The \"fully crossed\" design has important structural gaps.  The paper claims a fully-crossed design but several elements are not fully crossed: -  Exp-1 (MMLU) uses 3 precisions x 6 prompts x 6 seeds x 3 temperatures x 4 orderings, but Exp-2 (GSM8K/ARC/HellaSwag) uses only 2 precisions x 2 temperatures. This means the cross-benchmark comparisons in Table 3 are not on equal footing -- MMLU has richer factorial coverage and more records (1,036,800 vs 230,400 per benchmark). -  Hardware is only crossed in Exp-3 (MMLU), not in the multi-benchmark experiments. The separability claim therefore rests on a single benchmark. -  The 14B extension (Exp-5) uses 2 precisions only, not the full factorial. Claiming \"scale invariance\" from a reduced design on one benchmark is an overstatement. -  These design imbalances mean the pooled analyses implicitly weight MMLU more heavily. The paper should be transparent about which claims rest on full versus partial factorial evidence. W2.  200 items is potentially insufficient for stable higher-order interaction estimates.  With 200 items per benchmark and up to 12 variance components (Table 1), some interaction terms (especially 3-way and higher) are estimated from thin margins. The SEs in Table 1 are reported but several CIs are wide relative to the point estimates (e.g., ordering x item: 1.4% with CI [ 0.8, 2.0]; seed: 0.1% with CI [ 0.0, 0.2 ]). The paper does not report whether REML convergence diagnostics were checked, whether negative variance estimates were encountered and how they were handled (boundary constraints or set to zero), or whether bootstrap CIs were used as a robustness check. For a G-theory study, these are standard reporting requirements (Brennan 2001, Chapter 8). W3.  The 0.5% separability threshold is arbitrary and not well-justified.  The paper defines separability as direct infra x method interactions <0.5% of total variance, and the observed value is exactly 0.5% (Table 5). This is a razor-thin pass. The threshold is not derived from any established criterion in G-theory or psychometrics. Furthermore, \"0.5% of total variance\" is a relative measure that depends on the magnitude of item_ id variance -- if items were held fixed (eliminating 56% of variance), the same absolute interaction magnitude would represent ~ 1.1% of the remaining variance. The paper should either: (a) justify the threshold from first principles or prior literature, (b) report the result on an absolute scale (raw variance component values), or (c) frame it as a continuous quantity rather than a binary pass/fail. W4.  \"4 models pooled\" analysis conflates model-level and condition-level variance.  Pooling 4 models into a single variance decomposition (Table 1) is problematic because model is not a random facet in the same sense as prompt or seed -- these are 4 specific models, not a random sample from a model population. The pooled analysis implicitly treats model differences as part of the residual or item_ id component. The per-model analyses (Table 2) partially address this, but the headline numbers (58.4% item_ id) come from the pooled analysis. If model were included as a facet, model x item interactions could absorb substantial variance currently attributed to item_ id. The paper should either: (a) include model as a facet and report model x item interactions, or (b) report per-model results as primary and pooled as secondary, with clear caveats. W5.  D-study projections do not propagate estimation uncertainty.  The D-study budget tables report point estimates of G for each allocation but do not provide confidence intervals on G itself. Since G is a function of estimated variance components, and those components have non-trivial SEs (Table 1), the projected G values inherit estimation uncertainty. A G=0.90 projection could easily be G=[ 0.85, 0.95 ] given the component SEs. Without propagated uncertainty, the specific budget recommendations (e.g., \"600 items + 3 prompts + 2 seeds\") appear more precise than warranted. Bootstrap or delta-method CIs on projected G values are standard in D-study practice. W6.  The fine-tuning extension (RoBERTa-large on 4 NLU tasks) is a weak generalizability probe.  RoBERTa-large is a 355M encoder model fine-tuned on classification tasks -- architecturally and procedurally very different from 7-14B decoder models evaluated via generation. Claiming that \"item dominance extends to fine-tuning\" based on this single architecture on classification tasks is a stretch. The fine-tuning facet structure is also quite different (seed, LR, data shuffle, GPU, precision vs. prompt, seed, temperature, ordering, precision, hardware), making direct comparison of variance shares across paradigms (Table 10) potentially misleading. This extension would be more convincing with at least one generative fine-tuning setting (e.g., SFT of a 7B model). W7.  Missing dual-metric analysis undermines a key design decision.  The project's decisions.yaml (D002) records a deliberate decision to adopt dual-metric analysis (binary correct + text exact match) as a core methodology, noting that text exact match produces fundamentally different variance structure (prompt x item dominant at 37.5%, G=0.975). This analysis is entirely absent from the paper. Its omission is concerning because: (a) it would substantially complicate the \"item dominance\" narrative (item_ id may not dominate under text exact match), and (b) it was identified as a methodological strength. If the dual-metric analysis was dropped, the paper should justify why; if it was never completed, the paper should acknowledge that variance structure is metric-conditional. W8.  Only 2 GPU types for the hardware facet.  The hardware facet has only 2 levels (RTX PRO 6000 + one other GPU). In G-theory, variance component estimates for facets with very few levels are unstable. With k=2 levels, the hardware main effect and hardware x item interaction have 1 degree of freedom each, providing minimal power to detect non-zero components. The 0.6% hardware main effect could easily be noise. The paper should acknowledge this limitation more prominently rather than drawing strong conclusions about hardware effects from 2 GPUs. Questions for Authors Q1. How were negative variance component estimates handled in REML? Were any components estimated as negative and subsequently constrained to zero? If so, which components and in which experiments? This is critical for interpreting the small components (seed: 0.1%, ordering: 0.3%). Q2. The paper reports 1,036,800 records for Exp-1 as 4 models x 3 precisions x 6 prompts x 6 seeds x 3 temperatures x 4 orderings x 200 items. Was model included as a facet in the REML estimation, or were records from 4 models simply concatenated? If concatenated, model-level variance is confounded with item_ id and residual. Please clarify the exact mixed model specification. Q3. The separability test uses data from Exp-3 (691,200 records on MMLU only). Were separability tests conducted on the other 4 benchmarks? If not, the separability claim is benchmark-conditional, which undermines its generality. Q4. Table 1 components sum to approximately 95.5% (58.4+16.8+6.1+5.8+2.9+1.8+1.4+0.9+0.7+0.3+0.3+0.1=95.5). What accounts for the remaining ~ 4.5%? Higher-order interactions? Confounded terms? This should be explained. Q5. The D002 decision explicitly adopted dual-metric (binary correct + text exact match) analysis as a core methodology, noting that text exact match yields G=0.975 with a completely different variance hierarchy. Why was this analysis excluded from the paper? Does item dominance hold under text exact match? Q6. For the fine-tuning G-study, was item treated as a random facet in the same way as for inference? In fine-tuning, all training items are used for training, and item_ id refers to test items. Is the item_ id variance in Table 10 comparable across the two paradigms? Q7. The paper uses vLLM 0.9.2 with V0 enforce_ eager. Were any experiments run with V1 or batch-invariant kernels to quantify how much the engine choice itself contributes to the variance decomposition? Given the engine confound discovery, the variance estimates are conditional on this specific engine configuration. Minor Issues M1.  Table 1 column headers : \"SE\" and \"95% CI\" are not defined in the table caption. Are SEs computed via REML information matrix, jackknife, or bootstrap? The method matters for interpretation. M2. Summary This paper applies Generalizability Theory (G-theory) to decompose variance sources in LLM evaluation across five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), six models (4 at 7--9B, 2 at 14B), and approximately 4 million evaluation records. The design crosses infrastructure facets (numerical precision, GPU hardware) with methodology facets (prompt template, random seed, temperature, option ordering) and a measurement facet (item selection). Three claims are advanced: (1) item dominance is benchmark-conditional, following a monotonic 35pp gradient from knowledge retrieval (56%) to complex reasoning (21%); (2) direct infrastructure x methodology interactions are negligible ( <0.3%), confirming separability; (3) D-study reproducibility budgets reverse across task types (MMLU is item-limited, GSM8K is seed-limited), rendering universal evaluation recipes illusory. Eight experiments are presented, including a model-as-facet reanalysis, item resampling stability test, multi-hardware separability test, 14B scale extension, RoBERTa fine-tuning study, LayerCast precision mitigation, and MATH benchmark extension. 2. Methodology Assessment 2.1 G-Theory Application The application of G-theory is broadly correct and represents a natural fit for the research question. The crossed random-effects design, with item as the measurement facet and prompt/seed/temperature/ordering/precision as crossed facets, is the canonical G-theory setup for studying measurement dependability. The paper correctly distinguishes G-studies (variance decomposition) from D-studies (projection under alternative designs), which is the primary advantage of G-theory over standard ANOVA. However, there are several methodological concerns: (a) Object of measurement is underspecified.  In classical G-theory, the \"object of measurement\" (the entity whose score you want to generalize) must be clearly defined. In educational testing, this is typically the person. Here, the paper appears to treat benchmark accuracy as the object, but accuracy is an aggregate over items -- not a single observation. The paper decomposes item-level binary responses (correct/incorrect), which means the effective object of measurement is the  item-level response . The G coefficient then measures how well item-level responses generalize across facet conditions. This is a valid but nonstandard application. The paper should explicitly state what universe score is being estimated and what generalization is being made. The current framing conflates \"reliability of a benchmark score\" with \"stability of item-level responses across conditions,\" and these are different quantities. (b) Model-as-fixed vs. model-as-facet transition is handled well but incompletely.  The paper correctly identifies that pooling across models inflates item_ id (from 56% to 49.2% on MMLU when model is added as a facet). The model x item interaction (10.2%) is properly extracted. However, the paper does not discuss whether model should be treated as random or fixed from a G-theory perspective. With only 4 models drawn from a specific population (7-9B instruction-tuned open-weight models), the \"random\" assumption implies these 4 are a random sample from some universe of models -- a dubious claim given the deliberate selection. If model is fixed, model x item is not an error component but a systematic interaction, and the G coefficient computation changes. The paper should discuss this inferential scope issue. (c) Henderson Method I vs. III naming inconsistency.  The paper claims \"Henderson's Method III (expected mean squares)\" in Section 3.1, but the balanced fully-crossed design used here would typically employ Henderson Method I (which uses Type-I sums of squares and expected mean squares for balanced designs). Method III is Searle's approach for unbalanced designs. For the balanced design in exp-001, Method I is both simpler and more appropriate. This is either a naming error or an implementation concern -- the paper should clarify which method was actually used and verify consistency with the code. (d) Binary response variable creates floor/ceiling artifacts.  All primary analyses use binary correct/incorrect as the response. For items near 0% or 100% accuracy across conditions, variance is mechanically compressed (a Bernoulli variable with p near 0 or 1 has low variance). This means item_ id partially reflects the  range  of item difficulties rather than genuine measurement-relevant variance. The logprob analysis in Appendix B (item_ id drops to 42.8%) partially addresses this, but it is relegated to a 4-line appendix rather than being integrated into the main analysis. A continuous response variable would provide a more principled decomposition, and the paper should discuss the implications of using binary outcomes for variance component estimation. 2.2 Crossed/Nested Design Appropriateness The fully crossed design for MMLU (exp-001) is the gold standard for G-theory and is correctly specified. All facet levels are combined with all other facet levels, enabling clean estimation of all main effects and two-way interactions. The reduced designs for non-MMLU benchmarks (2 precisions x 2 temperatures vs. 3 x 3 for MMLU) are a pragmatic budget-driven decision but create a methodological asymmetry that is inadequately discussed. Variance percentages are  relative to total variance , and the total variance changes when you remove facet levels. Removing the FP32 precision level (which shows the highest deviation post-confound-fix) and the third temperature level changes the denominator of all percentage calculations. The cross-benchmark gradient (Table 4) compares percentages from designs with different factorial structures, which is a validity concern. The paper should either: (a) report a sensitivity analysis re-running MMLU with the reduced 2x2 design to confirm the gradient holds under matched designs, or (b) explicitly discuss why the design asymmetry does not invalidate the comparison. 2.3 Bootstrap Procedures The bootstrap procedure (1,000 item-level resamples) is appropriate in principle for constructing CIs on variance components, as parametric CIs for variance components in mixed models are notoriously unreliable. However: (a) Resampling items with replacement in a balanced design creates duplicates.  With 200 items and replacement, each bootstrap draw contains approximately 127 unique items (by the coupon collector / birthday problem). Duplicate items have identical response vectors across all conditions, violating the independence assumption in the ANOVA decomposition. This likely  deflates  the variability of item_ id estimates (making CIs too narrow), because the resampled datasets have artificially correlated item effects. A cluster bootstrap that resamples item-condition blocks without re-indexing duplicates, or a delete-d jackknife, would be more appropriate. The tight CI widths (4-6pp) should be interpreted with this caveat. (b) Nested bootstrap for D-study projections is not described.  The D-study projections in Table 11 presumably require computing variance components for each bootstrap sample and then projecting G under hypothetical designs. This is a two-stage procedure (bootstrap variance components -> project G), and the uncertainty in G projections depends on the joint distribution of all variance components, not just item_ id. The paper reports CIs on item_ id but not on D-study projections. The claim that \"420 items suffice for G >= 0.90 on MMLU\" has no associated uncertainty -- but given the bootstrap CIs on item_ id (46.1-52.3%), the projected item count for G >= 0.90 could range substantially. This uncertainty should be reported. 3. Experimental Rigor 3.1 Exp 1b: Item Resampling Stability The resampling stability test uses 1 model (Llama-3.1-8B) x 1 benchmark (MMLU) x 3 independent 200-item samples x 54 conditions per sample = 32,400 records. The CV of 4.1% on item_ id across samples is reassuring but has limited generalizability: -  Only 1 model tested.  The paper claims item resampling stability as a general property, but models with different accuracy distributions (e.g., Mistral-7B at 64.1% vs. Gemma-2 at 69.1%) might show different resampling sensitivity. A model near the population mean difficulty could show lower CV than one at the extremes. -  Only 3 samples.  A CV computed from 3 data points has essentially no statistical power. The standard error of a CV from n=3 is enormous. The paper would be better served by reporting the bootstrap distribution of variance components (which they have from exp-004, 1000 resamples) as the stability analysis, rather than the 3-sample CV. -  Only MMLU.  The critical question is whether resampling stability holds for GSM8K and MATH, where item_ id is much lower (21-25%) and closer to competing components. A CV of 4.1% on a 55% estimate is comfortable (55 +/- 2.3pp). But a CV of 4.1% on a 21% estimate would be 21 +/- 0.9pp -- still rank-1, but now within striking distance of temp x item at 20.8%. The resampling stability argument is weakest precisely where it matters most (reasoning benchmarks), and it is not tested there. Recommendation:  Replace the 3-sample CV with the bootstrap CI analysis from exp-004, and extend item resampling stability to at least one reasoning benchmark (GSM8K or MATH). 3.2 200-Item Sample Size Using 200 stratified items per benchmark is a reasonable choice that balances statistical power against computational cost. The stratification (by MMLU subject, presumably by difficulty for other benchmarks) ensures representative coverage. However: -  For MMLU (14K total items), 200 items is 1.4% of the pool -- adequate for stable percentage-based decompositions. -  For GSM8K (1,319 items in the test set), 200 items is 15.2% -- a much larger fraction, which reduces the effective resampling space. -  For MATH (5,000 items in the test set), 200 items is 4% -- again adequate. -  For ARC-Challenge (1,172 items), 200 items is 17.1%. The paper does not discuss how the item pool size interacts with the variance decomposition. When sampling 15-17% of the pool (GSM8K, ARC), the resampling stability results from MMLU (1.4% sampling fraction) may not transfer. This should be acknowledged. 3.3 Hardware Experiment (Exp 3): Confounds The multi-hardware study uses 2 GPU types. This is a minimal design for estimating hardware effects. Specific concerns: -  n=2 GPU types provides 1 degree of freedom for the hardware main effect.  This is barely identifiable in a variance decomposition. The hardware main effect (0.4%) and hardware x item (1.6%) estimates are based on between-GPU differences that could reflect any systematic difference between the two specific GPUs (driver version, cooling, memory controller characteristics, vLLM kernel selection), not hardware architecture per se. -  The paper does not specify the second GPU type.  The review context mentions \"RTX PRO 6000 + second GPU\" but the paper says only \"2 GPU types.\" For a claim about hardware separability to be meaningful, readers need to know whether these are architecturally similar (e.g., two Ampere-class GPUs) or substantially different (e.g., Ampere vs. Hopper). Two GPUs from the same architecture family would underestimate hardware variance. -  No confound control for driver/CUDA version differences between GPUs.  If the two GPUs run different CUDA toolkit versions or vLLM builds, observed differences reflect the software stack, not the hardware. Despite these limitations, the separability conclusion (<0.3% direct infra x method) is robust: even if hardware variance is underestimated due to limited GPU diversity, the  interaction  with methodology would need to be orders of magnitude larger to matter. The null result is defensible. 3.4 Fine-Tuning Experiment (Exp 6): RoBERTa Using RoBERTa-large for the fine-tuning study is a significant architectural mismatch. The inference experiments use 7-14B decoder-only autoregressive models on generation tasks; the fine-tuning experiment uses a 355M encoder-only model on classification tasks. The facets are also different (learning rate and data shuffle replace prompt template and temperature). This means: -  The cross-paradigm comparison (Table 13) compares variance percentages from incomparable designs. Item_ id being rank-1 in both does not constitute evidence of cross-paradigm generalization -- it could reflect the fact that any assessment with varying item difficulties will show item dominance, which is a tautological property of the design rather than an empirical finding. -  The claim that \"infrastructure effects are negligible in fine-tuning too\" is trivially expected for RoBERTa-large, which has no autoregressive error accumulation and was trained in FP32/FP16. -  The 1,728 fine-tuning runs (432 per task x 4 tasks) is a reasonable scale, but the number of  items  per evaluation is not specified. If each run evaluates the full dev/test set, the item-level observation count is much larger than 1,728. The experiment adds limited value to the core narrative.  Fine-tuning a decoder LLM (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B with LoRA on GSM8K, crossing seed x learning rate x data shuffle x items) would directly test cross-paradigm generalization. The current RoBERTa experiment tests a different claim entirely: that G-theory can decompose fine-tuning variance in encoder-only classification, which is unsurprising given that the same framework has been used in educational testing (which also involves classification-like assessments). 3.5 14B Scale Extension (Exp 5) With n=2 models (Qwen3-14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B), this experiment has minimal statistical power for any claim about scale effects. The two models differ in both scale and architecture: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B is a reasoning-distilled model with fundamentally different training objectives than Qwen3-14B. Scale and training methodology are fully confounded. The finding that both 14B models fall within the 8B range for item_ id is reassuring but does not demonstrate scale invariance -- it demonstrates that these two specific 14B models have similar variance profiles to the four 8B models. The elevated temp x item (8.8%) and seed x item (5.2%) for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B is attributed to \"reasoning distillation introducing implicit chain-of-thought tendencies\" (Section 8.1) -- this is a plausible but untestable hypothesis from n=1. The experiment contributes at best weak corroborating evidence. Two more 14B models (ideally from different training paradigms) would make the scale claim credible. 3.6 LayerCast (Exp 7) This is a null result experiment: LayerCast adds 0.03% precision variance, which is negligible. The experiment is methodologically clean but its contribution is marginal -- it confirms that precision is not a major concern (already established by exp-001 post-confound-fix) and evaluates a specific mitigation technique. For the paper's core claims, it is dispensable. Its inclusion creates a breadth-over-depth tradeoff that weakens the overall narrative. 4. Statistical Concerns 4.1 CV = 4.1% from 3 Samples The original review context described CV = 33% from 3 samples -- the paper now reports CV = 4.1%, which is a dramatic improvement, presumably reflecting better stratification and larger item counts in the revised design. However, a CV computed from n=3 is a point estimate with essentially no precision. The 95% CI on a CV from 3 observations is extremely wide (roughly 0.7x to 5x the point estimate under normal assumptions). The paper should not present CV = 4.1% as a precise number but rather as \"CV  < 15%\" or similar bounded claim. 4.2 Bootstrap with 1,000 Resamples 1,000 bootstrap resamples is adequate for percentile-based 95% CIs (Monte Carlo error approximately 0.5pp for the tail quantiles). The concern is not the number of resamples but the resampling unit: resampling items with replacement in a balanced design creates duplicate observations that violate independence assumptions in the ANOVA decomposition used within each bootstrap iteration. This is a known problem in bootstrap variance component estimation. The bias direction is toward underestimating CI width. 4.3 D-Study Projection Uncertainty D-study projections are deterministic functions of variance components: given estimated components, the projected G under any hypothetical design is a closed-form calculation. The uncertainty comes entirely from the variance component estimates. The paper reports CIs on item_ id (Table 8) but not on D-study projections. This is a significant omission. Paper Summary The paper applies Generalizability Theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation, conducting multi-benchmark crossed-facet variance decompositions across five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MATH), six models (4x7-9B + 2x14B), two GPU architectures, and multiple levels of precision, prompt template, seed, temperature, and answer ordering. Over 3 million evaluation records are analyzed. Three claims are made: (1) a benchmark-conditional variance gradient where item dominance ranges from 48% (MMLU) to 28% (MATH) under model-as-facet analysis; (2) infrastructure x methodology separability at the aggregate level ( <0.5% on knowledge benchmarks, rising to 3% on math-generation benchmarks); (3) metric-conditional, benchmark-specific reproducibility budgets via D-study projections. Extensions cover 14B models, RoBERTa fine-tuning, LayerCast precision mitigation, and three scoring metrics. 2. Methodological Soundness 2.1 G-Theory Framework Application Largely correct, with one significant improvement over Dream #1.  The revised paper treats model as a crossed random facet (Section 4.4 / Table 5), which was the most critical methodological concern in the prior review. This properly separates model×item interaction (16-22%) from pure item variance and residual. The 4pp systematic reduction across all benchmarks is plausible and consistent with psychometric expectation when objects of measurement have heterogeneous difficulty profiles. Henderson Method III vs. REML.  The paper uses Henderson Method III (expected mean squares) as primary estimation with REML as sensitivity check. This is defensible: Henderson III is unbiased for balanced designs, and the design is nearly balanced (fully crossed within each experiment). The reported max divergence of 2.1pp with preserved rank ordering is reassuring. However: -  Concern:  Henderson Method III can produce negative variance component estimates for near-zero components. The MATH table (Table 22 in the imagined experiments) shows a negative \"other\" entry (-1.5%), which is characteristic of this issue. The paper should explicitly state how negative estimates are handled (set to zero? redistributed? left as-is?). This matters for the separability claim where infra×method components are near zero — a negative estimate truncated to zero looks different from a genuinely zero estimate. -  Concern:  The G-theory formula presented in Equation 2 is simplified. The actual D-study formula for a multi-facet crossed design with 5+ facets involves many more terms. The paper should either present the full formula used or cite a specific implementation (e.g., GeneralizIT package). The simplified formula risks misleading readers about how D-study projections were actually computed. 2.2 Crossed Random-Effects Assumptions Items as random facet:  Justified. The 200 items per benchmark are sampled (stratified) from larger pools (MMLU: 14,042; ARC: 2,590; GSM8K: 1,319; HellaSwag: 10,042; MATH: 5,000). The random-facet assumption requires that observed items are exchangeable draws from a universe of admissible observations. Stratified sampling strengthens this by ensuring subject/topic coverage. Model as random facet:  Partially justified. Four 7-9B models from different families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral) are treated as exchangeable draws from the universe of \"7-9B instruction-tuned LLMs.\" This is defensible but arguable — the model universe is not well-defined, and four models provide limited degrees of freedom for estimating model-related variance components. The 14B extension (2 models) is even more constrained. The paper should acknowledge that model-as-facet with k=4 yields imprecise estimates of model variance components and that the model universe is narrowly defined (open-weight, instruction-tuned, 7-9B). Prompt as random facet:  The 6 prompt templates are described but their generation process matters for the random-effects assumption. If they were systematically designed to vary specific dimensions (e.g., formality, instruction explicitness), they may not represent random draws from a prompt universe. The paper should clarify whether prompt templates were generated to be representative (supporting random effects) or to maximize diversity (which biases variance estimates upward). Seed as random facet:  Clearly justified — seeds are arbitrary integers drawn from a large space. Temperature as random facet:  Problematic. With only 2-3 levels (e.g., 0, 0.5, 1.0), treating temperature as a random facet is statistically dubious — these are specific points chosen to span the parameter range, not random draws from a temperature distribution. Temperature is better modeled as fixed. If treated as random, the variance estimates carry extreme uncertainty with 2-3 df. The paper should address this. Ordering as random facet:  Four orderings (ABCD, BCDA, CDAB, DABC) — these are systematic rotations, not random draws. The random-effects assumption is defensible only if one argues these represent exchangeable draws from the universe of possible orderings, which is reasonable for 4-option MC but should be noted. 2.3 Variance Estimation for Binary Data Critical methodological question.  Binary correct (0/1) data violates the normality assumption underlying standard G-theory variance component estimation. Henderson Method III and REML both assume continuous, approximately normal response variables. For binary data: -  Variance components are bounded by the Bernoulli variance p(1-p), creating ceiling effects for items near p=0 or p=1. -  Item-level variance is mechanically linked to item difficulty — easy and hard items contribute less variance by construction, inflating the apparent dominance of \"mid-difficulty\" items. -  The paper's finding that item_ id is the largest variance source is partially an artifact of using binary scoring on items with heterogeneous difficulty. This is the well-known \"item difficulty confound\" in classical test theory. The text-exact-match metric (also binary) and logprob metric (continuous) provide useful sensitivity checks. The logprob result (item_ id = 55%) is methodologically cleaner because the response variable is continuous, avoiding the binary data issue. The paper should discuss the binary data limitation explicitly and note that logprob scoring provides the most methodologically sound variance decomposition. 3. This is the richest design and supports all claimed decompositions. The V0 enforce_ eager control eliminates the engine confound — this is excellent experimental hygiene. Cross-benchmark (Exp 3): Adequate but reduced.  2 precisions × 2 temperatures (vs. 3×3 on MMLU). The reduction is justified by compute constraints but creates an asymmetry: FP32 is absent from cross-benchmark experiments, meaning the precision facet is restricted to BF16/FP16 (which differ minimally). The claimed cross-benchmark gradient in precision effects (MMLU 3.0% vs. GSM8K 1.0%) is confounded with the different precision levels tested. This should be explicitly acknowledged. Multi-hardware (Exp 4): Adequate.  2 GPU types is the minimum for estimating hardware effects. With 1 df for hardware main effect, the estimate is necessarily imprecise. The paper correctly frames hardware findings as directional rather than definitive. Item resampling (Exp 2): Well-designed.  Three independent stratified draws with different seeds. The CV=0.19 (paper) or CV=0.19 (imagined experiments) on item_ id is an important honesty result. However, three draws provide only a rough estimate of resampling variability — 10+ draws would be more convincing, though the compute cost may be prohibitive. Fine-tuning (Exp 7): Adequate for its scope.  432 runs per task × 4 tasks = 1,728 total. The fully crossed design (seed × LR × shuffle × GPU × precision) is clean. The RoBERTa-large choice is acknowledged as a limitation (encoder-only, classification). This experiment is best framed as a conceptual extension rather than a direct generalization. 3.2 Missing Controls and Confounds 1.  Batch size / sequence length confound.  vLLM batches requests dynamically. If different benchmark items produce different output lengths (especially GSM8K/MATH with CoT), batch composition may vary, introducing an unmodeled variance source that gets absorbed into residual or item interactions. The paper uses \"default vLLM settings\" which is realistic but means batch-level nondeterminism is present. 2.  Prompt template × benchmark interaction.  The same 6 prompt templates are used across benchmarks, but their appropriateness may vary by task. A prompt template that works well for MMLU factual recall may be poorly suited for GSM8K math reasoning. This could inflate prompt×item interactions on some benchmarks for reasons unrelated to the \"prompt sensitivity\" construct. 3.  Item difficulty distribution differs across benchmarks.  MMLU items span a wide difficulty range; GSM8K items at 8B model scale cluster near 0.4-0.6 accuracy; MATH items are heavily bimodal (trivial or impossible for 8B models). These distributional differences mechanically affect how much variance is attributable to items vs. interactions. The paper's \"cognitive complexity\" explanation for the cross-benchmark gradient is plausible but not the only explanation — difficulty distribution differences could account for part of the pattern. 4.  Stratified sampling details.  The paper mentions stratified sampling across 57 MMLU subjects, but the stratification scheme for other benchmarks (GSM8K difficulty levels? For generation-based scoring, the method of extracting answers from generated text is a potential confound. Different regex/parsing strategies could produce different binary scores for the same generation. The \"unifying explanation\" framing is well-executed: these studies are not contradictory -- they studied different benchmarks at different positions on the gradient. However, the finding that item_ id dominates is expected from measurement theory (Brennan, 2001, Ch. 3). Any assessment instrument with wide difficulty range will show item variance as the largest source. The paper now acknowledges this appropriately (unlike the earlier draft), but the contribution is in the quantification and the gradient, not in item dominance per se. Claim 2 (Confirmatory separability): Low novelty, moderate utility. This is a confirmatory null result. The nuanced decomposition into direct vs. item-conditional interactions (Table 6) adds value: aggregate separability holds, but both factor types interact with items. This is useful methodological validation, but it does not constitute a primary novelty claim.
